---
title: "3. Elliptic curves"
engine: pari-gp
format: html
---

`ellinit` takes the five coefficients of a long Weierstrass equation,
$y^2 + a_1xy + a_3y = x^3 + a_2x^2 + a_4x + a_6$, and precomputes everything
else once. Here is $X_0(11)$, the smallest conductor there is:

```{gp}
E = ellinit([0, -1, 1, -10, -20]);
[E.disc, E.j]
```

The conductor confirms it:

```{gp}
ellglobalred(E)[1]
```

## Rank and torsion

```{gp}
ellanalyticrank(E)
```

Rank zero, so the group of rational points is finite — and it is cyclic of
order 5:

```{gp}
elltors(E)
```

## Counting points mod p

`ellap` returns $a_p = p + 1 - \#E(\mathbb{F}_p)$, the coefficient that
carries all the arithmetic:

```{gp}
[[p, ellap(E, p)] | p <- primes(8)]
```

The same numbers are the coefficients of the $L$-series, which is the content
of modularity:

```{gp}
ellan(E, 15)
```

Hasse's bound says $|a_p| \le 2\sqrt{p}$; for $p = 10^6+3$ that leaves a
window of about `{gp} round(4*sqrt(1000003))` values, and gp finds the right
one immediately:

```{gp}
ellap(E, 1000003)
```

## A curve with points on it

Rank one instead, so there is an infinite supply of rational points:

```{gp}
C = ellinit([0, 0, 1, -1, 0]);
[ellglobalred(C)[1], ellanalyticrank(C)]
```

Start from $(0,0)$ and add it to itself; the coordinates grow fast, which is
what the canonical height measures:

```{gp}
P = [0, 0];
[ellmul(C, P, 2), ellmul(C, P, 3)]
```

```{gp}
[ellheight(C, P), ellheight(C, ellmul(C, P, 3))]
```

The second is nine times the first, because the height is a quadratic form.
